'''''Hedera helix''''', simply '''ivy''', or '''common ivy''', '''English ivy''',<ref name=EPPO>{{cite web |title=''Hedera helix'' |url=https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/HEEHE |publisher=[[European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization]] (EPPO) |access-date=29 December 2025}}</ref> '''European ivy''', '''King's choice ivy''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Araliaceae]]. It is [[native plant|native]] to most of Europe and parts of western Asia. Ivy is a clinging [[evergreen]] [[vine]] that grows on tree trunks, walls, and fences in gardens, waste spaces, and wild habitats. Ivy is common as an [[ornamental plant]], but escaped plants become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] outside its native range. Ivy has considerable [[Hedera#Cultural symbolism|cultural significance and symbolism]].

Synonyms include ''Hedera acuta'', ''Hedera arborea'' ('tree ivy'),<ref>Bean, W. J. (1978) ''Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles'' Volume 2.</ref> ''Hedera baccifera'', and ''Hedera grandifolia.''<ref>[[International Plant Names Index]]</ref> Other common names are bindwood and lovestone.

==Description==
''Hedera helix'' is an [[evergreen]] climbing plant, growing to {{convert|20|-|30|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} high where suitable surfaces ([[tree]]s, [[cliff]]s, [[wall]]s) are available, and also growing as [[groundcover]] where no vertical surfaces occur. It climbs by means of [[aerial root]]lets with matted pads which cling strongly to the substrate. The ability to climb on surfaces varies with the plant's variety and other factors: ''H. helix'' prefers non-reflective, darker and rough surfaces with near-neutral [[pH]]. It generally thrives in a wide range of [[soil pH]] with 6.5 being ideal, prefers moist, shady locations and avoids exposure to direct sunlight, the latter promoting drying out in winter.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.plantsrescue.com/tag/hedera-helix-jubilee/|title=Plants & Flowers—Hedera helix Jubilee|access-date=2015-08-20}}</ref>

The [[leaves]] are alternate, {{convert|50|–|100|mm|0|abbr=on}} long, with a {{convert|15|–|20|mm|1|abbr=on}} [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]; they are of two types, with [[leaf shape|palmately]] five-lobed juvenile leaves on creeping and climbing stems, and unlobed cordate adult leaves on fertile flowering stems exposed to full sun, usually high in the crowns of trees or the top of rock faces.

The [[flower]]s are produced from late summer until late autumn, individually small, in {{convert|3|to|5|cm|in|abbr=on|adj=mid|-diameter}} [[umbels]], greenish-yellow, and very rich in [[nectar]], an important late autumn food source for bees and other insects.

The [[fruit]] are purple-black to orange-yellow [[berry (botany)|berries]] {{convert|6|–|8|mm|1|abbr=on}} in diameter, ripening in late winter,<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|page=1136}}</ref> and are an important food source for many birds.

One to five [[seed]]s are in each berry, which are dispersed after being eaten by birds.<ref name="Metcalfe"/><ref name="McAllister"/><ref name="flora"/>

===Subspecies===
The three [[subspecies]] are:<ref name="Metcalfe"/><ref name="Ackerfield"/>

*'''''H. h. helix'''''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paulsen |first1=Evy |last2=Christensen |first2=Lars P. |last3=Andersen |first3=Klaus E. |date=April 2010 |title=Dermatitis from common ivy ( Hedera helix L. subsp. helix ) in Europe: past, present, and future |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0536.2009.01677.x |journal=Contact Dermatitis |language=en |volume=62 |issue=4 |pages=201–209 |doi=10.1111/j.1600-0536.2009.01677.x |pmid=20236156 |issn=0105-1873|url-access=subscription }}</ref> − central, northern and western Europe, plants without [[rhizomes]], purple-black ripe fruit,
*'''''H. h. poetarum''''' Nyman (syn. ''Hedera chrysocarpa'' Walsh) (Italian ivy, poet's ivy) − southeast Europe and southwest Asia (Italy, Balkans, Turkey), plants without rhizomes, orange-yellow ripe fruit,
*'''''H. h. rhizomatifera''''' McAllister − southeast Spain, plants [[rhizome|rhizomatous]], purple-black ripe fruit.

The closely related species ''[[Hedera canariensis]]'' and ''[[Hedera hibernica]]'' are also often treated as subspecies of ''H. helix'',<ref name="flora"/><ref name="Europe"/> though they differ in [[chromosome]] number and so do not [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridise]] readily.<ref name="McAllister"/> ''H. helix'' can be best distinguished by the shape and colour of its leaf [[trichome]]s, usually smaller and slightly more deeply lobed leaves and somewhat less vigorous growth, though identification is often not easy.<ref name="flora"/><ref>[http://website.lineone.net/~margaret_cole/News4/holly&ivy.htm The Holly and the Ivy. ''Shropshire Botanical Society Newsletter'' Autumn 2000: page 14]</ref>

== Etymology ==
The genus name {{lang|la|[[Hedera]]}} is the [[Classical Latin]] word for 'ivy', which is cognate with Greek {{lang|grc|χανδάνω}} ({{lang|grc-Latn|khandánō}}) 'to get, grasp', both deriving ultimately from [[Proto-Indo-European]] {{lang|ine-x-proto|gʰed(h)-}} 'to seize, grasp, take'.<ref> Lionel Horton-Smith,''[https://www.jstor.org/stable/288121 ΚΙΣΣΟΣ and Hedera],'' [[The American Journal of Philology]],   16,1 1895 pp.38-45 p.38 </ref> The [[botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''helix'' was borrowed into Latin from [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|ἕλιξ}} ({{lang|grc-latn|helix}}), '[[helix]]', 'spiral'.. The binomial in its entirety thus has the meaning "the clinging plant that coils in spirals (helices)".<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 |location=United Kingdom |page=224}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2018 |title=Helical (Helix) |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/helical#etymonline_v_34234 |access-date=15 November 2018 |publisher=Online Etymology Dictionary, Douglas Harper}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Hedera helix in Hennef (Sieg), Germany.jpg|thumb|Common ivy climbing a fencepost in [[Hennef (Sieg)|Hennef]], Germany]]
[[File:Hedera helix clinging on Platanus x hispanica, Agde, Hérault.jpg|thumb|right|Common ivy clinging on a [[Platanus × hispanica|London plane]] in [[Agde]], France]]
The range of ''Hedera helix'' is from Ireland northeast to southern Scandinavia, south to Portugal, and east to [[Ukraine]], [[Iran]] and northern [[Turkey]]. In Britain, it is very common and widespread, but absent from the [[Isle of Man]] and [[Channel Islands]].<ref>Poland J, Clement EJ. 2020. ''The Vegetative Key to the British Flora''. John Poland, Southampton, Second Edition. {{ISBN|978-0-9560144-2-9}}</ref>

== Invasive species ==
{{see also|Hedera#Problems and dangers}}

Like other exotic species, ivy has predominantly been spread by human action. ''H. helix'' is labeled as an [[invasive species]] in parts of the world.

===Australia===
The Centre for Invasive Species Solutions lists ''Hedera helix'' as a weed across southern, especially south-eastern Australia, and local councils provide advice on how to remove it and limited services for removal.<ref name="WeedsAus" /> It is officially scheduled as a weed in [[Western Australia]] and the [[Australian Capital Territory]].<ref name="WeedsAus" /> ''Hedera helix'' is the only species of ivy bearing the legal status of 'declared weed' in Australia; however, it may be the case that much of what is identified as invasive "English Ivy" in Australia is in reality ''[[Hedera hibernica]]''.<ref name="WeedsAus">{{cite web |title=Hedera helix |url=https://weeds.org.au/profiles/english-ivy/ |website=Weeds Australia |publisher=Centre for Invasive Species Solutions |access-date=20 January 2025}}</ref>

===Canada===
Although common as a winter holiday decoration, ''H. helix'' is invasive and is a pathogen alternate host in [[British Columbia]].<ref name="BC-ISC-holiday" /><ref name="ISC-BC" />

===New Zealand===
''H. helix'' has been listed as an "environmental weed" by the Department of Conservation since 1990.<ref>{{cite book |last=Howell |first=Clayson |url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/drds292.pdf |title=Consolidated list of environmental weeds in New Zealand |date=May 2008 |publisher=Department of Conservation |isbn=978-0-478-14413-0 |series=DRDS292 |location=Wellington |access-date=2009-05-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530024209/http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/drds292.pdf |archive-date=2009-05-30 }}</ref>

===United States===
In the [[United States]], ''H. helix'' is considered weedy or invasive in a number of regions and is on the official [[noxious weed]] lists in [[Oregon]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]], with its sale being banned in both states.<ref name="USDA">[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=HEHE USDA Plants Profile: ''Hedera helix'']</ref><ref>[http://www.oregonlive.com/business/index.ssf/2010/02/oregon_bans_sale_of_english_iv.html Oregon bans sale of English ivy, butterfly bushes]</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weeds/english-ivy |title=English ivy |publisher=Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board |access-date=12 September 2025}}</ref><ref>[http://www.pesticide.org/pubs/alts/ivy/englishivy.html Controlling English Ivy] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081210184939/http://www.pesticide.org/pubs/alts/ivy/englishivy.html|date=2008-12-10}}. Northwest Coalition for Alternatives to Pesticides.</ref> Like other invasive vines such as [[Kudzu in the United States|kudzu]], ''H. helix'' can grow to choke out other plants and create "ivy deserts". State- and county-sponsored efforts are encouraging the destruction of ivy in forests of the [[Pacific Northwest]] and the [[Southern United States]].<ref name="nil">{{cite web |title=Ivy chasers in a league of their own |url=http://www.portlandtribune.com/sustainable/story.php?story_id=117797294153983800 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110608040401/http://www.portlandtribune.com/sustainable/story.php?story_id=117797294153983800 |archive-date=2011-06-08 |access-date=2008-11-27 |work=Pamplin Media Group}}</ref><ref name="Arlington">[http://www.arlingtonva.us/Departments/ParksRecreation/scripts/parks/ivy.pdf Controlling English Ivy] Arlington County, Virginia Department of Parks, Recreation and Community Resources.</ref> Ivy can easily escape from cultivated gardens and invade nearby parks, forests and other natural areas via squirrels and birds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Invasive to Avoid: English Ivy |url=https://wildlife.ca.gov/Conservation/Plants/Dont-Plant-Me/English-Ivy |access-date=2022-12-06 |publisher=California Department of Fish and Wildlife}}</ref>

=== Control, eradication, and recovery ===
Once ivy is established it is very difficult to control or eradicate. If left untreated it will crowd out other ground cover plants and can choke out and kill shrubs and overstory trees.<ref name="Oregon State University-2008">{{Cite web |last=Oregon State University |date=September 2008 |title=Invasive Weeds in Forest Land: English Ivy Hedera helix |url=https://www.oregon.gov/ODA/programs/Weeds/Meetings/Documents/English%20Ivy%20Forum%202016/EnglishIvyManagementResourcePacket.pdf |access-date=29 January 2023 |website=Oregon.gov}}</ref>

Tested and successful methods of control are mechanical removal and chemical applications.<ref name="Oregon State University-2008" /> Chemical eradication includes the use of [[2,4-Diaminotoluene|2,4-D amine]], [[glyphosate]], and [[Metsulfuron-methyl|metsulfuron]], with metsulfuron being the most effective on ''H. helix''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Qian |last2=Wehtje |first2=Glenn |last3=Gilliam |first3=Charles H. |last4=McElroy |first4=J. Scott |last5=Sibley |first5=Jeff L. |date=1 September 2013 |title=English Ivy (Hedera helix) Control with Postemergence-Applied Herbicides |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/invasive-plant-science-and-management/article/abs/english-ivy-hedera-helix-control-with-postemergenceapplied-herbicides/318A2957EB6907658D3E02931FAB3573 |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=411–415 |doi=10.1614/IPSM-D-13-00009.1 |bibcode=2013IPSM....6..411Y |issn=1939-7291|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Mechanical removal typically involves hand pulling and has been found to be more environmentally beneficial in the long term than chemical removal. A study has shown that after removal, seed addition significantly increased species richness, diversity, and density on pulled ivy, while seed addition had no benefits on chemically sprayed ivy. This is likely due to the dead roots still occupying the soil after spraying, which are removed when pulling.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Biggerstaff |first1=Matthew S. |last2=Beck |first2=Christopher W. |date=1 July 2007 |title=Effects of Method of English Ivy Removal and Seed Addition on Regeneration of Vegetation in a Southeastern Piedmont Forest |url=http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.1674/0003-0031%282007%29158%5B206%3AEOMOEI%5D2.0.CO%3B2 |journal=The American Midland Naturalist |language=en |volume=158 |issue=1 |pages=206–220 |doi=10.1674/0003-0031(2007)158[206:EOMOEI]2.0.CO;2 |issn=0003-0031|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

After mechanical removal, the recovery of native species can be significant after one year from resprouting and germination. However, ivy produces fruits that can be spread by birds, so continuous management after recovery is still necessary to prevent invasion from recurring in the same location or nearby.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jiménez-Hernández |first1=Héctor Adrián |last2=Bonilla-Valencia |first2=Leticia |last3=Martínez-Orea |first3=Yuriana |last4=Zamora-Almazan |first4=Mara Jessica |last5=Espinosa-García |first5=Francisco Javier |last6=Castillo-Argüero |first6=Silvia |date=2023-07-05 |title=Effects of Hedera helix L. removal on the understory early regeneration in an oak temperate forest in Mexico City |journal=Ecological Processes |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=31 |doi=10.1186/s13717-023-00443-y  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2023EcoPr..12...31J |issn=2192-1709}}</ref>

One study found that during the next growing season after H. h''elix'' removal, herbaceous native plants were more abundant and diverse, while shrubs and ferns had either no increase or a decrease in abundance and diversity. This can be due to herbaceous plants having viable seeds buried in the soil, while ferns are slow-growing, and existing shrubs may not bear seeds from limited sunlight in the forest.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bierzychudek |first=Paulette |date=2020-10-01 |title=Passive recovery of an urban forest in the Pacific Northwest after removal of invasive plants |journal=Urban Ecosystems |language=en |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=1023–1038 |doi=10.1007/s11252-020-00966-8 |bibcode=2020UrbEc..23.1023B |issn=1573-1642}}</ref>

Areas of invasion can be identified using [[Lidar|LiDAR detection]], which has been measured at around 82% accuracy, with better accuracy in places with less [[canopy cover]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chance |first1=Curtis M. |last2=Coops |first2=Nicholas C. |last3=Plowright |first3=Andrew A. |last4=Tooke |first4=Thoreau R. |last5=Christen |first5=Andreas |last6=Aven |first6=Neal |date=2016-10-21 |title=Invasive Shrub Mapping in an Urban Environment from Hyperspectral and LiDAR-Derived Attributes |journal=Frontiers in Plant Science |language=English |volume=7 |page=1528 |doi=10.3389/fpls.2016.01528  |doi-access=free|issn=1664-462X |pmc=5073150 |pmid=27818664 |bibcode=2016FrPS...07.1528C }}</ref>

=== Damage to trees ===
Ivy can climb into the canopy of young or small trees in such density that the trees fall over from the weight,<ref name="Arlington" /> a problem that does not normally occur in its native range.<ref name="Metcalfe" /> In its mature form, dense ivy can destroy habitat for native wildlife and creates large sections of solid ivy where no other plants can develop.<ref name="Arlington" /> It is also thought to be a reservoir for [[Bacterial leaf scorch|leaf scorch bacteria]].<ref>{{cite web |title=English ivy, Hedera helix Apiales: Araliaceae |url=https://www.invasive.org/browse/subinfo.cfm?sub=3027}}</ref> However, the UK Woodland Trust considers that it does not damage trees and hence does not require removal.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ivy (Hedera helix) - British Wildflowers |url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/trees-woods-and-wildlife/plants/wild-flowers/ivy/}}</ref> The ivy also blocks the sun from the trees that need it for photosynthesis.{{verify source|date=November 2025}}

==Cultivation==
[[File:Entrance to High Castle in Malbork.jpg|thumb|Ivy-covered entrance to [[Malbork Castle]] in Poland]]
[[File:Starr-071024-9905-Hedera helix-variegated leaves-Enchanting Floral Gardens of Kula-Maui (24895451805).jpg|thumb|Variegated ivy leaves growing at the [[Enchanted Floral Gardens of Kula, Maui]]]]
Ivy is widely cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]]. Within its native range, the species is greatly valued for attracting wildlife. The flowers are visited by over 70 species of nectar-feeding insects, and the berries eaten by at least 16 species of birds. The foliage provides dense evergreen shelter, and is also browsed by deer.<ref name="Metcalfe"/><ref>[http://www.plantforwildlife.ccw.gov.uk/plants/common-ivy-hedera-helix.aspx?x=6897 Plant for Wildlife: Common Ivy (Hedera helix)] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006141415/http://www.plantforwildlife.ccw.gov.uk/plants/common-ivy-hedera-helix.aspx?x=6897 |date=2011-10-06 }}</ref>

In Europe, it is frequently planted to cover walls<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fassadengruen.de/uw/kletterpflanzen/uw/efeu/efeu.htm|title=Efeu Hedera - ein Alleskönner|language=de|access-date=2015-08-20}}</ref> and the Bavarian government recommends growing it on buildings for its ability to cool the interior in summer, while providing insulation in winter, as well as protecting the covered building from soil moisture, temperature fluctuations and direct exposure to heavy weather.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stmwi.bayern.de/fileadmin/user_upload/stmwivt/Themen/Energie_und_Rohstoffe/Merkblaetter_aktuell/30_Hinweise_Energiesparen_Bauwerksbegruenung_gesichert.pdf|title=Bauwerksbegrünung - Hinweise zum Energiesparen|publisher=Bayerisches Staatsministerium für Wirtschaft und Medien, Energie und Technologie|language=de|date=September 2014|access-date=2015-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150820130721/http://www.stmwi.bayern.de/fileadmin/user_upload/stmwivt/Themen/Energie_und_Rohstoffe/Merkblaetter_aktuell/30_Hinweise_Energiesparen_Bauwerksbegruenung_gesichert.pdf|archive-date=2015-08-20}}</ref> Further uses include weed suppression in plantings, beautifying unsightly facades and providing additional green by growing on tree trunks.

However, ivy can be problematic. It is a fast-growing, self-clinging climber that is capable of causing damage to brickwork, guttering, etc., and hiding potentially serious structural faults, as well as harbouring unwelcome pests. Careful planning and placement are essential.<ref name=rhs/>

==Toxicity and medical uses==
Ivy berries are somewhat poisonous to humans, but extracts from ivy leaves are part of current [[Cough Medicine|cough medicines]].<ref>European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (2017). [https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-report/final-assessment-report-hedera-helix-l-folium-revision-2_en.pdf Assessment report on Hedera helix L., folium], pp. 5-16</ref> A 2020 evidence review found that ''H. helix'' preparations "may be a therapeutic option for treating early symptoms of respiratory tract infections", saying that "the best effectiveness for ''H. helix'' preparations has been proven for coughing, as an expectorant and to reduce the frequency and intensity of cough. Only weak evidence was found for all other researched symptoms."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=Larisa AJ |last2=Leach |first2=Matthew |last3=Anheyer |first3=Dennis |last4=Brown |first4=Danielle |last5=Carè |first5=Jenny |last6=Lauche |first6=Romy |last7=Medina |first7=Daen N |last8=Pinder |first8=Tobey-Ann |last9=Bugarcic |first9=Andrea |last10=Steel |first10=Amie |date=December 2020 |title=The effects of Hedera helix on viral respiratory infections in humans: A rapid review |journal=Advances in Integrative Medicine |language=en |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=222–226 |doi=10.1016/j.aimed.2020.07.012 |pmc=7424313 |pmid=32837900}}</ref>

In the past, the leaves and berries were taken orally as an [[expectorant]] to treat cough and [[bronchitis]].<ref>Bown. D. (1995). ''Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses''. Dorling Kindersley, London. {{ISBN|0-7513-0203-1}}</ref> In 1597, the British herbalist [[John Gerard]] recommended water infused with ivy leaves as a wash for sore or watering eyes.<ref>{{Cite book  | last =Gerard  | first =John  | editor1-last =Woodward  | editor1-first =Marcus | title =Gerard's Herbal: The History of Plants  | publisher =Crescent Books  | year =1985  | location =New York  | isbn = 978-0-517-46470-0  }}</ref> The leaves can cause severe [[contact dermatitis]] in some people.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Jøhnke | first1 = H | last2 = Bjarnason | first2 = B | year = 1994 | title = Contact dermatitis allergy to common ivy (Hedera helix L.) | journal = Ugeskr. Laeger | volume = 156 | issue = 25| pages = 3778–3779 | pmid=8059459}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Boyle | first1 = J. | last2 = Harman | first2 = R. M. H. | year = 2006 | title = Contact dermatitis to Hedera helix (Common Ivy) | journal = Contact Dermatitis | volume = 12 | issue = 2| pages = 111–112 | doi = 10.1111/j.1600-0536.1985.tb01067.x | pmid = 3987251 | s2cid = 29719245 }}</ref> People who have this allergy (strictly a [[type IV hypersensitivity]]) are also likely to react to carrots and other members of the [[Apiaceae]] as they contain the same allergen, [[falcarinol]].

Previous studies showed that the ''H. helix'' extract contains [[α-hederin]] and β-hederin, [[falcarinol]], didehydrofalcarinol, [[rutin]], [[caffeic acid]], [[chlorogenic acid]], [[emetine]], [[Kaempferol 3-O-rutinoside|nicotiflorin]], hederasaponin B and hederacoside C.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Medeiros |first1=Jorge R. |last2=Medeiros |first2=Helena |last3=Mascarenhas |first3=Carla |last4=Davin |first4=Laurence B. |last5=Lewis |first5=Norman G. |date=2002 |title=Bioactive components of Hedera helix. |url=https://repositorio.uac.pt/handle/10400.3/164 |journal=Arquipélago |issn=0873-4704}}</ref> However, only three extracted components were detectable more than 1.5% in the ''Hedera helix'' leaves (hederacoside C 15.69%, chlorogenic acid 2.07%, and rutin 1.62%). Other components were detectable in very few amounts (< 1%) or not detectable in some studies.<ref>Alkattan, A., Alameer, R., Alsalameen, E. et al. Safety of English ivy (Hedera helix) leaf extract during pregnancy: retrospective cohort study. DARU J Pharm Sci (2021). https://doi.org/10.1007/s40199-021-00415-7</ref>

Owing to the large number of [[saponin]]s in the leaves and fruits of ''H. helix'', it is mildly poisonous to animals like rabbits and can lead to [[anemia]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ivy leaf extract,Hedera helix,Hederagenin,Hederacoside C,cough|date=6 November 2014 |url=https://herbnutritionals.com/herbal-extracts/ivy-leaf/|access-date=2021-03-31|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Pratt|first=Amy|date=2020-03-20|title=20 Plants that are Poisonous to Rabbits|url=https://bunnylady.com/poisonous-plants/|access-date=2021-03-31|website=The Bunny Lady|language=en-US}}</ref>

In a hunting session for resources, birds would restrict the number of ivy berries ingested because of the moderate toxicity. However, berries are taken in larger quantities in the spring once they have ripened and lost some of their toxicity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Strelau |first1=M. |last2=Clements |first2=D.R. |last3=Benner |first3=J. |last4=Prasad |first4=R. |date=2018-10-01 |editor-last=Willenborg |editor-first=Christian |title=The Biology of Canadian Weeds: 157. Hedera helix L. and Hedera hibernica (G. Kirchn.) Bean |url=http://www.nrcresearchpress.com/doi/10.1139/cjps-2018-0009 |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |language=en |volume=98 |issue=5 |pages=1005–1022 |doi=10.1139/cjps-2018-0009 |issn=0008-4220|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Extract of ''H. helix'' is highly effective in resisting [[fire blight]]. It has been observed to significantly inhibit the fire blight pathogen ''E. amylovora'' for up to 7 days, with similar effectiveness as applying [[acibenzolar-S-methyl]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baysal |first1=Ö. |last2=Zeller |first2=W. |date=2004-12-01 |title=Extract of Hedera helix induces resistance on apple rootstock M26 similar to Acibenzolar-S-methyl against Fire Blight (Erwinia amylovora) |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0885576505000494 |journal=Physiological and Molecular Plant Pathology |volume=65 |issue=6 |pages=305–315 |doi=10.1016/j.pmpp.2005.03.003 |bibcode=2004PMPP...65..305B |issn=0885-5765|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Use as building façade==
When used as a [[Façade|building façade]], ivy provides both [[Building insulation|insulation]] and weather protection.<ref name="coombes">{{Cite journal |last=Coombes |first=Martin A. |last2=Viles |first2=Heather A. |last3=Zhang |first3=Hong |date=2018-06-29 |title=Thermal blanketing by ivy (''Hedera helix'' L.) can protect building stone from damaging frosts |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-28276-2 |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1 |doi=10.1038/s41598-018-28276-2|doi-access=free |issn=2045-2322|pmc=6026199 }}</ref> Its roots dry the soil due to frequent need for water, inhibiting moisture on walls, but its robust self-climbing rootlets can be problematic if not managed correctly, causing damage to mortar and leaving permanent gaps on surfaces.<ref name=coombes/>

''Hedera helix'' grows vigorously and clings by means of fibrous roots, which develop along the entire length of the stems. These are difficult to remove, leaving an unsightly "footprint" on walls, and possibly resulting in expensive resurfacing work. Additionally, ivy can quickly invade [[Rain gutter|gutter]]s and roof spaces, lifting tiles and causing blockages. It also harbors mice and other creatures. The plants have to be cut off at the base, and the stumps dug out or killed to prevent regrowth.<ref name="rhs">{{cite web|title=Ivy on buildings and fences |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/prevention-protection/ivy-on-buildings|publisher=The Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=15 August 2026|date=2026}}</ref>

With the insulating effects of ''Hedera helix'', it can reduce the deterioration of limestone and other stone surfaces by protecting them from freezing events. ''H. helix'' may reduce the frequency of freezing events 26%, the duration of freezing events by 34%, and the severity of freezing events by 32%, along with a noticeable reduction of damage to the limestone material.<ref name=coombes/>

== Mechanism of attachment ==
''Hedera helix'' is able to climb relatively smooth vertical surfaces, creating a strong, long lasting adhesion with a force of around 300 nN.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xia|first1=Lijin|last2=Lenaghan|first2=Scott C.|last3=Zhang|first3=Mingjun|last4=Wu|first4=Yu|last5=Zhao|first5=Xiaopeng|last6=Burris|first6=Jason N.|last7=Stewart|first7=C. Neal|date=2011-03-01|title=Characterization of English ivy (Hedera helix) adhesion force and imaging using atomic force microscopy|journal=Journal of Nanoparticle Research|language=en|volume=13|issue=3|pages=1029–1037|doi=10.1007/s11051-010-0091-3|issn=1388-0764|bibcode=2011JNR....13.1029X|s2cid=18080100}}</ref> This is accomplished through a complex method of attachment starting as [[adventitious root]]s growing along the stem make contact with the surface and extend root hairs that range from 20 to 400 μm in length. These tiny hairs grow into any small crevices available, secrete glue-like [[nanoparticle]]s, and [[lignification|lignify]]. As they dry out, the hairs shrink and curl, effectively pulling the root closer to the surface.<ref name="Melzer-2010">{{Cite journal|last1=Melzer|first1=Bjorn|first2=Tina |last2=Steinbrecher |first3=Robin |last3=Seidel |first4=Oliver |last4=Kraft |first5=Ruth |last5=Schwaiger |first6=Thomas |last6=Speck |date=12 May 2010|title=The attachment strategy of English Ivy: a complex mechanism acting on several hierarchical levels|journal=The Journal of the Royal Society Interface |volume=7 |issue=50 |pages=1383–1389 |language=en|doi=10.1098/rsif.2010.0140 |pmc=2894893 |pmid=20462880}}</ref>

The glue-like substance is a nano composite adhesive that consists of uniform spherical nanoparticles 50–80 nm in diameter in a liquid polymer matrix.  Chemical analyses of the nanoparticles detected only trace amounts of metals, once thought to be responsible for their high strength, indicating that they are largely organic. Recent work has shown that the nanoparticles are likely composed in large part of [[arabinogalactan]] proteins (AGPs), which exist in other plant adhesives as well.<ref name="Lenaghan-2013">{{Cite journal|last=Lenaghan|first=Scott|date=October 2013|title=Isolation and chemical analysis of nanoparticles from English ivy|journal=The Journal of the Royal Society Interface |volume=10 |issue=87 |doi=10.1098/rsif.2013.0392 |pmid=23883948 |pmc=3757999 }}</ref>
